result:
At 4:17 every morning, the streetlights went out.

No one knew why. The town had replaced the wiring twice, installed timers, installed sensors, installed a man named Gerald whose entire job was to sit in a van and watch the lights. Still, at exactly 4:17, every lamp along Juniper Street blinked once and went dark.

It lasted for eleven seconds.

Eleven seconds was not long enough to be dangerous, though Mrs. Alvarez claimed she had nearly walked into a mailbox during the blackout of 1998. It was not long enough to interrupt anything important, except the bakery’s security camera, which recorded eleven frames of darkness every morning. The town council held a meeting about it, then another meeting to discuss the first meeting, and finally decided that the phenomenon was “electrically irregular but functionally harmless.”

People adjusted.

The newspaper delivery boy learned to coast through the darkness. The cats learned to stop crossing the road. The baker began pulling bread from the ovens at 4:16, just in case.

Then, one winter morning, the lights went out—and did not come back on.

For eleven seconds, the street held its breath.

For eleven minutes, the town waited.

By sunrise, every lamp on Juniper Street was still dark. The lamps on the neighboring streets worked perfectly. So did the traffic signals, porch lights, shop signs, and the enormous illuminated pharmacy cross that flickered green above the rooftops.

Only Juniper Street remained black.

That evening, children gathered beneath the dead lamps and dared one another to stand in the middle of the road. Adults came too, pretending they were merely passing by. At the corner, Gerald sat in his van with both hands resting on the steering wheel, staring at the control panel as if it had personally betrayed him.

At 9:00, someone noticed that the darkness was not empty.

There were stars in it.

Not above the street, where stars had always been, faint and distant beyond the town’s orange glow, but inside the dark circles beneath the lamps. Tiny points of silver shimmered in the glass, each one reflected from somewhere impossibly far away.

People looked up.

The sky was cloudy.

They looked back at the lamps.

Inside one of them, a constellation moved.

By midnight, the whole town had come to Juniper Street. No one spoke loudly. They stood shoulder to shoulder under the broken lights, watching galaxies turn slowly in the glass.

And at 4:17 the next morning, the lamps came back on.

The stars vanished.

But from then on, whenever the town grew too busy, too certain, too loud with the machinery of ordinary life, one lamp would fail. Then another. A small darkness would open somewhere, reminding everyone that the world was much larger than the part illuminated for them.

No one ever managed to repair that. Eventually, no one wanted to.
